deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a page of German lecture notes on ancient history, continuing the section '3. Geschichte des macedonischen Reichs und der griechischen Staaten, 323–146' begun on folio 176. The hand and genre suggest student notes from a history lecture, possibly of the Göttingen type such as Heeren's courses. Nothing on the page indicates Gauss's own mathematical work, and the hand may not be his.

Content, in order:
(1) After a four-year struggle, Cassander takes possession of Macedonia.
(2) In 319 BC Cassander flees to Antigonus in Asia, having first tried to strengthen his party in Macedonia and Greece.
(3) Nominally Arrhidaeus (Philip III) rules, but his wife Eurydice holds the greater share of power.
(4) Polyperchon recalls Olympias and withdraws the garrisons from several Greek cities.
(5) Polyperchon sends his son (Alexander) to Athens to remove Nicanor. A revolution follows in which Phocion dies.
(6) Cassander comes in person and sets 'Demetrius Valerius' (i.e. Demetrius of Phalerum) at the head of Athens. The notes say he governed for 11 years.
(7) Olympias returns with an army. Two 'brothers of Cassander' are executed, together with Eurydice and her husband, in 317.
(8) In 316 Olympias herself is executed, and Cassander becomes master of Macedonia.
(9) He marries Alexander's half-sister Thessalonice and founds Thessalonica in her honour. He also founds Cassandreia and restores Thebes.
(10) In 311 a general peace leaves Cassander in possession of Macedonia. He was supposed to put Alexander (IV) on the throne, but in 311 he had him killed together with his mother (Roxane).

There are no derivations to reconstruct.
errors: 'Demetrius Valerius' is a mishearing or miswriting of Demetrius Phalereus (of Phalerum). The next page spells it correctly as 'Phalereus'.
Demetrius of Phalerum governed Athens c. 317–307 BC, about 10 years. The note's '11 Jahr' is slightly off; some sources count inclusively.
Phocion did not simply die in a revolution. He was deposed, tried by the restored democracy and executed by hemlock in 318 BC.
'2 Brüder Cassanders' is doubtful. Diodorus records that Olympias killed Cassander's brother Nicanor (and desecrated the tomb of Iollas, another brother) along with about a hundred of his friends.
The murder of Alexander IV and Roxane is usually dated c. 310/309 BC, shortly after the peace of 311, rather than in 311 itself.

results.what: Narrative of the early Diadochi period (Cassander, Polyperchon, Olympias, Philip III Arrhidaeus and Eurydice, Phocion, Demetrius of Phalerum, the peace of 311)
results.modern_name: Hellenistic history: Wars of the Diadochi, 319–309 BC
results.usually_credited_to: Ancient sources (Diodorus XVIII–XIX, Plutarch's Phocion) and standard 18th/19th-century handbooks such as Heeren

deep.surprise_reason: These are ordinary history lecture notes on Macedonian history with no mathematical content. The material is textbook knowledge and has nothing to do with Gauss's mathematical work.

checkable.asserts: Demetrius of Phalerum's rule (317–307 BC) lasted about 10 years, not 11.
Consistent with the 'four-year struggle' after Alexander's death in 323, counted to 319.

transcription_corrections: Line 9: 'Als[?]' reads plausibly as 'Als'; the image shows 'Als' before 'Polysperchon seinen Sohn'.
'Demetrius Valerius' is indeed what is written, but the historical referent is Demetrius Phalereus.
Line 1 spelling 'Mazedonien' (with z) is as written. Later lines use 'Macedonien'.
'Euridice' (line 6) and 'Eurydice' (line 18) are both spelled as written in the manuscript.
